title: OQ-02: the Girard–Euler spherical excess formula
content: Girard's theorem identifies the area (in steradians) of a spherical triangle on the unit sphere with its **spherical excess** $S = A + B + C - \pi$. A fully self-contained proof needs a spherical-area (solid-angle) measure together with lune-area lemmas and a covering count — infrastructure Mathlib lacks at v4.26.0 (estimated >1000 lines). This file instead formalises the two arithmetic pillars every classical proof rests on, with 0 axioms and 0 sorries: finite additivity of the excess under geodesic subdivision, and the lune-covering reduction. The geometric inputs enter as theorem hypotheses, so every result is an unconditional, machine-checked implication.
prerequisites: Spherical geometry (geodesic triangles, dihedral angles, lunes)
Solid angle / area on the unit sphere

title: The spherical excess
content: `sphericalExcess A B C := A + B + C - π`, noncomputable because it references `Real.pi`. The `@[simp]` unfolding lemma and the symmetry lemma (the labelling of vertices is arbitrary) are recorded. Girard's theorem is the assertion that this quantity equals the triangle's area.

title: Pillar 1: excess is additive under a cevian subdivision
content: `sphericalExcess_additive_cevian`: a geodesic from vertex C to a point D on the opposite side AB splits △ABC into △ADC and △DBC. Given the vertex split `C = C₁ + C₂` and the supplementary relation `δ₁ + δ₂ = π` at the interior point D, the excesses of the two pieces sum to the excess of the whole. The proof is a single `linarith` after unfolding: the angle sums contribute `+ (δ₁ + δ₂) − 2π = +π − 2π = −π`, exactly reconstituting the whole-triangle excess. This finite additivity is the structural reason the excess behaves like an area.
prerequisites: The two geometric subdivision relations (taken as hypotheses)

title: Spherical polygon excess: quadrilateral and pentagon cases
content: `sphericalExcess_quadrilateral` proves a geodesic quadrilateral has area $\alpha+\beta+\gamma+\delta-2\pi$ by cutting along a diagonal (the angles at the two diagonal endpoints split). `sphericalExcess_pentagon` proves the $n=5$ case, area $=\sum\text{angles}-3\pi$, via a fan of two diagonals from one vertex into three triangles. Both confirm the general spherical polygon formula $\operatorname{area} = (\sum\text{angles}) - (n-2)\pi$, which follows from triangulating an $n$-gon into $n-2$ triangles and summing Girard's excess.
prerequisites: Diagonal/fan triangulation (angle splits taken as hypotheses)

title: Pillar 2: Girard's theorem from the lune covering
content: `girard_euler_from_lunes` derives `S = A + B + C - π` from the classical lune computation. Extending the triangle's three sides to great circles produces, at each vertex, an antipodal pair of lunes; a lune of dihedral angle θ has area 2θ, so the three pairs have combined areas 4A, 4B, 4C. These six lunes tile the sphere (area 4π) while covering the triangle T and its antipode T′ (each of area S) three times and every other point once, so their total area is also `4π + 4S`. Equating gives `4A + 4B + 4C = 4π + 4S`, hence Girard's formula by `linarith`. The lune-area and covering-count facts are the hypotheses; the arithmetic closure is the verified content.
prerequisites: Lune area = twice the dihedral angle (hypothesis)

title: Consequences: angle-sum dichotomy, flat limit, bounds, monotonicity
content: Five corollaries of Girard's formula. `pos_area_iff_angle_sum_gt_pi`: positive area ⟺ angle sum exceeds π (genuine spherical triangles are 'fat', a hallmark of positive curvature). `excess_eq_zero_iff`: zero excess ⟺ angle sum = π, recovering the Euclidean angle-sum theorem as the flat (zero-curvature) limit. `excess_nonneg_iff`: the non-negativity criterion. `excess_lt_two_pi`: each interior angle < π forces area < 2π, the hemisphere bound. `excess_strictMono_left`: the area is strictly increasing in any single opening angle.
prerequisites: Girard's formula (or the definition of excess)

title: Summary and honest scoping
content: 1 definition, 11 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms (`#print axioms` lists only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound). The geometric inputs of Girard's theorem appear as hypotheses, so the file proves the arithmetic backbone and lune reduction rather than a self-contained measure-theoretic proof — the missing piece (a Mathlib spherical-area measure with the lune-area lemma) is recorded as the principal open question.
